        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis.

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the task.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents you’ll need to create/modify.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone or push to the repo from here, but the commands below will do it for you on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you already have the repo locally, just `cd` into it.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & create/update files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create or overwrite `Dockerfile` at the repo root:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Maintainer
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

# Working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *Why node:18‑alpine?*  
> It’s lightweight, stable, and matches the typical Node.js version used in many tutorials.  
> If the repo uses a different Node version (check `package.json`), adjust the `FROM` line accordingly.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a `k8s` directory (if it doesn’t exist) and add a single combined manifest `deployment-service.yaml`:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment-service.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change if you use another registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> *Tip:*  
> If you prefer separate files (`deployment.yaml` + `service.yaml`), split the above YAML accordingly.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: ./Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
```

> **What this does**  
> * Checks out the repo.  
> * Builds the Docker image using the Dockerfile.  
> * Pushes the image to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`).  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` for authentication – no extra secrets needed.

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment-service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you added separate `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml`, add those instead.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions CI"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run on the next commit to `main`.

---

## Quick sanity check

1. **Dockerfile** – `docker build -t test-image .` should succeed.  
2. **Kubernetes** – `kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment-service.yaml` should create the deployment and service.  
3. **GitHub Actions** – Go to the *Actions* tab on GitHub; you should see the workflow run and finish successfully.

---

### What if the repo already had a Dockerfile or Kubernetes manifests?

- **Dockerfile** – If one exists, review it and replace the content with the snippet above (or merge changes).  
- **Kubernetes** – Same idea: replace or merge the existing manifests.  

Just make sure you keep any custom logic that the original repo might rely on.

---

That’s it! Once you run these commands, your repo will have a ready‑to‑use Dockerfile, Kubernetes deployment/service, and a CI pipeline that builds and pushes the image whenever you push to `main`. Happy coding!
